name: Boids

lumenary.blurb: A flock with three rules: keep apart, fly the same way, stay close. Each bird paints in the colour beneath it, so the flock slowly paints your picture.

facts.bestOn: Pictures with a dark background and bright shapes

why: A flock of starlings moves as one, with no leader and no plan. Craig Reynolds showed that three rules, applied by each bird to its neighbours only, are enough to give that behaviour. Add a pull toward the light parts of a picture, and a brush for each bird, and the flock slowly paints.
how: Give each bird a position and velocity, and let it see neighbours within 46 px at 720 px wide, found through a hash grid.
Separation: steer away from anything too close, growing strongly as it nears.
Alignment: steer toward the average heading of neighbours. Cohesion: steer toward their average position.
Add the gradient of the picture’s brightness, so birds climb toward light, plus a gentle push from the cursor and a little random force.
Clamp the speed between 0.45 and 1 times the top speed, wrap round at the edges like a torus, and paint with the colour under each bird.
history: Craig Reynolds presented boids (bird-oid objects) in 1986 and published the paper in 1987. Flocking of this kind was used for the swarm of bats and the army of penguins in Batman Returns in 1992, and Reynolds received a Scientific and Technical Academy Award in 1998. Similar rules guide drone swarms and crowd simulations.
uses: Crowds, flocks and schools in film and games
terms: A simulated bird-like agent following simple flocking rules.
A world that wraps round, so leaving one side re-enters the other.
paragraphs: Craig Reynolds showed in 1986 that the flocking of birds needs no leader, only three rules that each bird applies to its neighbours: separation (steer away from those too close), alignment (steer toward their average heading) and cohesion (steer toward their average position). The program applies them to birds that see the neighbours within 46 px (at 720 px wide), found through a hash grid. Alignment has strength 1.6 times the flocking slider, cohesion 1.2 times it, and separation is a push away from anything within 0.38 of the sensing distance, growing to 220 as it nears. A little random force is added, and the speed is clamped between 0.45 and 1 times the top speed. The world wraps round like a torus.

Two forces come from the picture and from you. The pull toward light is the gradient of the picture’s normalised lightness (a Sobel gradient), times the pull slider, so birds climb toward the bright parts. The pointer attracts birds within 40% of the picture’s width, and repels them while pressed. Most of all, each bird paints. On every step it draws a line from its last position to its new one on a persistent canvas, in the colour of the picture beneath it, and the flock slowly paints the picture. The comet look fades that canvas by 14% each step so only trails remain, and shows the birds as small arrowheads. The painting is done inside the step, so the first-frame thumbnail has paint on it.

equations.tex: \mathbf f_i=1.6\,\Phi\,(\bar{\mathbf v}-\mathbf v_i)+1.2\,\Phi\,(\bar{\mathbf x}-\mathbf x_i)+220\sum_{j:\,d_{ij}<0.38\,\rho}\Big(1-\frac{d_{ij}}{0.38\,\rho}\Big)\frac{\mathbf x_i-\mathbf x_j}{d_{ij}}
equations.note: Alignment, cohesion and separation; Φ is the flocking slider, ρ the sensing distance, and the bars are averages over neighbours.

equations.tex: \mathbf f_i\mathrel{+}=\sigma\,\nabla L(\mathbf x_i)+\text{noise},\qquad \mathbf v_i\leftarrow\mathbf v_i\,\frac{\operatorname{clip}\big(\lVert\mathbf v_i\rVert,\ 0.45\,v_{\max},\ v_{\max}\big)}{\lVert\mathbf v_i\rVert}
equations.note: The pull toward light (σ the pull slider) and the speed limit.

presets.text: Comet mode shows each bird as a bright streak.
A tight flock swirls into dense clouds.
Strong pull toward light paints the bright shapes first.
